Hebron (Place)
HEE-brun
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Chevron (H2275), possibly "association, league, confederacy" (from chavar, "to join"); anciently also called Kirjath-arba ("city of Arba"). A town in the hill country of Judah, among the oldest in the world.

Biblical Definition

Hebron was an ancient city in the hill country of Judah, deeply bound up with the patriarchs and with King David. Abraham dwelt by the oaks (plain) of Mamre at Hebron, where he built an altar (Gen 13:18) and where the LORD appeared to him and announced the birth of Isaac (Gen 18). When Sarah died at Hebron, Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah there from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place (Gen 23) — the first piece of the promised land that the patriarchs owned, and the tomb in which Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were all buried (Gen 49:31; 50:13). Thus Hebron holds the bones of the patriarchs, the down-payment of the land-promise. In the conquest, Hebron was given to Caleb, who at eighty-five drove out the giants (the sons of Anak) and took it as his inheritance, the reward of his wholehearted following of the LORD (Josh 14:6-15). It became one of the cities of refuge and a Levitical city (Josh 20:7; 21:11). Most notably, Hebron was David's first capital: there he was anointed king over Judah, and there he reigned seven and a half years before capturing Jerusalem and reigning over all Israel (2 Sam 2:1-4; 5:1-5). It was also at Hebron that Absalom raised the standard of his rebellion (2 Sam 15:7-10). Hebron thus links the patriarchs (in the tomb of Machpelah) to the Davidic kingdom (in David's first throne) — a place of burial, of inheritance won by faith (Caleb), and of the beginning of the kingdom from which the Son of David would come.

Webster 1828 Definition

An ancient city in Judah; Abraham dwelt at Mamre nearby and bought the cave of Machpelah there for the patriarchs' burial (Gen 23); Caleb's inheritance won by wholehearted faith (Josh 14); David's first capital, anointed king there (2 Sam 2; 5).

HEBRON (PLACE), proper noun. Hebrew Chevron (H2275), possibly "association"; anciently Kirjath-arba; a town in the hill country of Judah.

Abraham dwelt by Mamre at Hebron, built an altar (Gen 13:18), and was told of Isaac's birth (Gen 18).

He bought the cave of Machpelah there for Sarah's burial — the patriarchs' tomb (Gen 23; 49:31; 50:13).

Caleb's inheritance, won at 85 by driving out the giants, the reward of his wholehearted following of the LORD (Josh 14:6-15).

David's first capital, anointed king over Judah there, reigning 7.5 years before taking Jerusalem (2 Sam 2:1-4; 5:1-5); Absalom's rebellion began there (2 Sam 15).

Key Scripture

Genesis 23:19-20 — "And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan. And the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace by the sons of Heth."

Joshua 14:13-14 — "And Joshua blessed him, and gave unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh Hebron for an inheritance. Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb... because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel."

2 Samuel 5:3-5 — "So all the elders of Israel came to the king to Hebron; and king David made a league with them in Hebron before the LORD: and they anointed David king over Israel... In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months."

Genesis 49:31 — "There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah."

Modern Corruption

Hebron is corrupted only when its dense patriarchal and Davidic significance is flattened, when the tomb of Machpelah is read as mere antiquity rather than the down-payment of the land-promise, or when Caleb's wholehearted faith that won Hebron is overlooked.

expand to see more

Down-payment-of-promise missed. The cave of Machpelah at Hebron was the first piece of the promised land the patriarchs actually owned — Abraham bought it, in full and public transaction, as a burial place. There he laid Sarah, and there were laid Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah. The detail is theologically weighty: the patriarchs died in faith, not having received the promises, but the tomb of Machpelah was the pledge that the land would be theirs (Heb 11:13). They were buried in the land of promise as a down-payment of the inheritance their seed would possess. To read Machpelah as mere antiquity is to miss the faith that bought a grave as a claim on God's promise.

Hebron has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the faith of the patriarchs who bought a burial-place as a pledge of the promise, and the wholehearted faith of Caleb who at eighty-five drove out the giants to claim Hebron as his inheritance — "because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel" (Josh 14:14). Hebron is a place won and held by faith, and the first throne of the Davidic kingdom from which the Son of David would come.

An ancient city in Judah; Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah there for the patriarchs' burial (Gen 23); Caleb's inheritance won by wholehearted faith (Josh 14); David's first capital (2 Sam 2; 5).
